title: Claim Social Security at 62 in Texas (2026): Real Break-Even & Tax Math
metaDescription: See what claiming Social Security at 62 really buys you in Texas: 2026 monthly benefit math, break-even vs. waiting to 70, state tax treatment, and Medicare strategy.
narrative: Claiming at 62 is the earliest possible age in this pair of ages, and it is the maximum-flexibility play: the smallest monthly check, taken as early as SSA allows, in exchange for the most years of cash flow and the least portfolio drawdown while you wait. At an illustrative $2,450/mo FRA benefit, claiming at 62 pays $1,715/mo ($20,580/yr) — that covers about 57% of a comfortable $3,000/mo budget in Texas, leaving a gap of roughly $385,500 in additional savings (4% rule) to close the rest. The honest trade-off against waiting to 70 is a fixed one: every year you claim early instead of at 70 gives up roughly 8% more guaranteed, inflation-linked income for life, but it also lets a bigger share of your portfolio stay invested and compounding instead of being drawn down to bridge the gap. In a lower-cost location like Texas (comfortable budget: $3,000/mo), that trade shifts in favor of claiming earlier than it would in a high cost-of-living metro, because the smaller check goes further and the portfolio-preservation math does more work per dollar.
tradeoffs: Monthly benefit at 62 (illustrative $2,450/mo FRA case): $1,715/mo, or $20,580/yr — 70% of the FRA-67 amount.
Covers 57% of Texas's comfortable cost of living; closing the rest needs about $385,500 in additional savings under the 4% rule.
Waiting instead to 70 raises the check to $3,038/mo, but only pays off after the 62-vs-70 break-even age — typically the late 70s to early 80s in nominal dollars.
No state income tax on Social Security or IRA/401(k) withdrawals.
taxNote: No state income tax on Social Security or IRA/401(k) withdrawals. 401(k)/IRA withdrawals still count toward provisional income at the federal level, which can make up to 85% of your Social Security taxable regardless of state.
medicareNote: Medicare works normally. Home insurance and property tax are the cost drivers. Part B runs $203/mo in 2026, with IRMAA surcharges above certain income thresholds.
